When IIA fails, or when the cases of a unit share unobserved tastes, the
multinomial logit is the restricted member of several families that
`polychoice` fits with the same interface. This vignette fits each of them,
shows how to compare them with the logit, and notes where their parameters are
identified only weakly.


``` r
library(polychoice)
```

## Nested logit

The two-level nested logit groups the alternatives into nests with an
inclusive-value parameter \(\lambda_m\) per nest; \(\lambda_m = 1\) for every
nest is the multinomial logit, and smaller values mean stronger correlation of
the unobserved utilities within the nest. The parameterization is the
utility-maximization-consistent one of McFadden (1978), the form that `mlogit`
and Stata's `nlogit` use, so results are comparable across software. Here the
Australian travel-mode data are grouped into fast and slow modes.


``` r
data("TravelMode", package = "AER")
TM <- TravelMode
TM$chosen <- as.integer(TM$choice == "yes")
nests <- list(fast = c("air", "train"), slow = c("bus", "car"))
m0 <- mnl(chosen ~ wait + vcost + travel + gcost | income + size, data = TM,
          id = "individual", alt = "mode")
mn <- nlogit(chosen ~ wait + vcost + travel + gcost | income + size, data = TM,
             id = "individual", alt = "mode", nests = nests)
#> Inclusive-value parameter(s) above 1 (lambda:fast): outside the range consistent with random-utility maximization for all covariate values; the nesting may be wrong or unnecessary (lr_test() against the mnl() fit).
summary(mn)
#> Nested logit (2 nests) 
#> Call: nlogit(formula = chosen ~ wait + vcost + travel + gcost | income + 
#>     size, data = TM, nests = nests, id = "individual", alt = "mode")
#> Alternatives: air, train, bus, car  (base: air)
#> 
#> Outcome equations (alternative:term):
#>                   Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> train:(Intercept)  1.12266    1.44876   0.775 0.438393    
#> train:income      -0.08694    0.02567  -3.386 0.000708 ***
#> train:size         0.77910    0.52134   1.494 0.135069    
#> bus:(Intercept)    0.10158    1.49349   0.068 0.945776    
#> bus:income        -0.03292    0.02062  -1.597 0.110274    
#> bus:size           0.45035    0.51447   0.875 0.381376    
#> car:(Intercept)   -5.13458    1.64663  -3.118 0.001819 ** 
#> car:income        -0.01996    0.01706  -1.170 0.241861    
#> car:size           0.49022    0.40260   1.218 0.223359    
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Generic coefficients (alternative-specific covariates):
#>         Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> wait   -0.126661   0.021141  -5.991 2.08e-09 ***
#> vcost  -0.072630   0.032583  -2.229  0.02581 *  
#> travel -0.013933   0.004646  -2.999  0.00271 ** 
#> gcost   0.065636   0.033150   1.980  0.04771 *  
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Inclusive-value parameters lambda (z tests are against 1 = multinomial logit; the joint test is lr_test() against the mnl() fit):
#>             Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)  
#> lambda:fast   1.7980     0.4091   1.950   0.0511 .
#> lambda:slow   0.7980     0.2265  -0.892   0.3726  
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Standard errors: analytic. Log-likelihood -165.223 on 15 parameters, 210 cases. AIC 360.45, BIC 410.65.
lr_test(m0, mn)
#> Likelihood-ratio test
#>   LR = 10.9286 on 2 df, p = 0.004235
```

The point estimates equal mlogit's. The standard errors do not: mlogit reports
outer-product (BHHH) standard errors for this model, which `se = "opg"`
reproduces (0.85 and 0.35 for the two inclusive-value parameters against the
0.41 and 0.23 of the observed information shown here). Which to report: the
observed information (the default) is the usual choice; the two estimates of
the information agree when the model is correctly specified and the sample is
large, so a gap of a factor of two, as here, is itself a warning about the
specification, and `se = "robust"` (the sandwich of the two) is the choice that
does not rest on it. Note also the value 1.80 for the fast nest: an
inclusive-value parameter above 1 lies outside the range consistent with
random-utility maximization for all covariate values (the fit says so in the
message printed above) and is itself evidence that this nesting is not the
right description of these data. `equal_lambda = TRUE` imposes one shared
inclusive-value parameter; a singleton nest's parameter does not enter the
likelihood and is fixed at 1. The parameters are estimated on the log scale
and reported on the natural scale with delta-method standard errors; the z
tests in the summary are against 1, and the joint test of IIA is the
likelihood-ratio test against the `mnl()` fit, as above.

With case-specific covariates only (the wide layout) the inclusive-value
parameters are identified only through the curvature of the inclusive values
and are recovered imprecisely; alternative-specific covariates identify them
sharply. The same holds for the HEV scales and the probit covariance below,
and the package's simulators (`rnlogit()`, `rhev()`, `rmnp()`) have a `gamma`
argument that generates such covariates in the long layout.

## Heteroskedastic extreme value

The HEV model (Bhat 1995) keeps independent Gumbel errors but lets their scale
differ by alternative (the base alternative's scale is 1); IIA is relaxed
through the scales. The choice probabilities are one-dimensional integrals
that the package evaluates to about ten digits by a trapezoidal rule, or by
adaptive Gauss-Kronrod quadrature when one alternative's scale is much smaller
than another's. A simulated long-layout example:


``` r
set.seed(15)
dh <- rhev(600, beta = cbind(b = c(0.5, -1, 0.8), c = c(-0.3, 0.6, -0.5)),
           scale = c(1, 0.6, 1.5), gamma = 1)
mh <- hev(chosen ~ w1 | x1 + x2, data = dh, id = "id", alt = "alt")
summary(mh)
#> Heteroskedastic extreme value model 
#> Call: hev(formula = chosen ~ w1 | x1 + x2, data = dh, id = "id", alt = "alt")
#> Alternatives: a, b, c  (base: a)
#> 
#> Outcome equations (alternative:term):
#>               Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> b:(Intercept)   0.3127     0.2463   1.270   0.2042    
#> b:x1           -1.4137     0.2864  -4.936 7.99e-07 ***
#> b:x2            1.1113     0.2591   4.289 1.79e-05 ***
#> c:(Intercept)  -0.2390     0.3037  -0.787   0.4313    
#> c:x1            0.5080     0.2250   2.258   0.0240 *  
#> c:x2           -0.3700     0.1919  -1.929   0.0538 .  
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Generic coefficients (alternative-specific covariates):
#>    Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> w1   1.1167     0.1995   5.598 2.17e-08 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Gumbel scale parameters (base alternative = 1; z tests are against 1; the joint test is lr_test() against the mnl() fit):
#>         Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)  
#> scale:b   0.6362     0.2825  -1.288   0.1977  
#> scale:c   1.6501     0.3822   1.701   0.0889 .
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Standard errors: analytic. Log-likelihood -426.029 on 9 parameters, 600 cases. AIC 870.06, BIC 909.63.
lr_test(mnl(chosen ~ w1 | x1 + x2, data = dh, id = "id", alt = "alt"), mh)
#> Likelihood-ratio test
#>   LR = 13.5651 on 2 df, p = 0.001133
```

A scale that runs to zero means that the alternative's utility is estimated
as deterministic relative to the others; the fit is flagged as a boundary fit,
and the standard errors are not interpretable. The search holds each log
scale within \(\pm 8\). The likelihood is usually flat beyond that; where it
still rises, the boundary warning says so, and the reported log-likelihood is
then below the model's supremum (the fit-quality flags in `?mnl`). The
travel-mode data are an example of a scale running to zero: the car scale goes
to zero, and the value that `mlogit` reports for that model is not its true
log-likelihood but an artifact of its quadrature (the package's verification
ledger has the details).

## Multinomial probit

The multinomial probit admits any covariance of the utility errors. Only
utility differences are identified, so the model is parameterized by the
covariance of the differences from the base alternative with its first element
fixed at 1 (Train 2009, section 5.2). With three alternatives the
probabilities are exact bivariate normal integrals; with more, the GHK
simulator with `draws` Halton draws per case is used.


``` r
set.seed(1)
dp <- rmnp(1500, beta = cbind(b = c(0.3, -0.6, 0.5), c = c(-0.2, 0.4, -0.3)),
           sigma = matrix(c(1, 0.6, 0.6, 1.5), 2), gamma = 1)
mp <- mnprobit(chosen ~ w1 | x1 + x2, data = dp, id = "id", alt = "alt")
summary(mp)
#> Multinomial probit (exact bivariate normal) 
#> Call: mnprobit(formula = chosen ~ w1 | x1 + x2, data = dp, id = "id", 
#>     alt = "alt")
#> Alternatives: a, b, c  (base: a)
#> 
#> Outcome equations (alternative:term):
#>               Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> b:(Intercept)  0.28684    0.05610   5.113 3.16e-07 ***
#> b:x1          -0.54203    0.05690  -9.525  < 2e-16 ***
#> b:x2           0.49601    0.05271   9.411  < 2e-16 ***
#> c:(Intercept) -0.17855    0.07288  -2.450   0.0143 *  
#> c:x1           0.48605    0.07211   6.740 1.58e-11 ***
#> c:x2          -0.24811    0.06216  -3.992 6.56e-05 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Generic coefficients (alternative-specific covariates):
#>    Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> w1   0.9956     0.0607    16.4   <2e-16 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Covariance of the utility differences from the base (first variance fixed at 1; z tests are against the iid values, variances 1 and covariances 0.5):
#>         Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)   
#> cov:c,b   0.8079     0.1065   2.891  0.00385 **
#> var:c     1.5448     0.2549   2.138  0.03256 * 
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Standard errors: analytic. Log-likelihood -856.531 on 9 parameters, 1500 cases. AIC 1731.06, BIC 1778.88.
```

The probit does not nest the logit, so the two are compared with `vuong()`
or the information criteria; probit coefficients are on a smaller scale
(the error-difference variance is 1 rather than \(\pi^2/3\)). The data were
drawn with covariance 0.6 and variance 1.5. In this sample the variance
estimate is close to its value, the covariance estimate about two standard
errors above it, and the slopes within about one standard error of the values
used to simulate them. In a recovery study of the same design (200 simulated data sets
at each of 1,500 and 3,000 cases, `verification/mnprobit_recovery_mc.R` in the
repository) the coefficient estimates average within 0.015 of those values
with 1,500 cases and within 0.010 with 3,000, the variance within 0.05 and
0.012 (a finite-sample bias), and the 95 percent Wald intervals cover in 90
to 97 percent of the data sets. The two departures at 3,000 cases beyond
Monte Carlo error, a slope bias of 0.010 and a coverage of 0.905, did not
recur on 200 fresh seeds, and fits of 200,000 cases recover every value
within two standard errors. Covariance
parameters are the noisiest part of a probit fit even with an
alternative-specific covariate, and they are fragilely identified from
case-specific covariates alone (Keane 1992): fits may then stop at a
near-singular covariance with a warning, and the covariance estimates should
not be interpreted. With four or more alternatives the GHK simulated
likelihood is not smooth near a singular covariance, so there the gradient
and the convergence check are unreliable too, and the boundary warning says
so (`?mnprobit`).


``` r
vuong(mp, mnl(chosen ~ w1 | x1 + x2, data = dp, id = "id", alt = "alt"))
#> Vuong test:  m1 = mp [ Multinomial probit (exact bivariate normal) ]
#>              m2 = mnl(chosen ~ w1 | x1 + x2, data = dp, id = "id", alt = "alt") [ Conditional logit ]
#> positive statistics favor m1
#> 
#>  correction statistic p_m1_better p_m2_better p_two_sided
#>         raw     2.205       0.014       0.986       0.027
#>         AIC     1.623       0.052       0.948       0.104
#>         BIC     0.078       0.469       0.531       0.938
```

## Random alternative-specific intercepts

When the cases of a unit (a respondent over several elections, a country
over years) share unobserved tastes, `remnl()` adds a normal random intercept
per unit in every non-base equation and integrates it out by adaptive
Gauss-Hermite quadrature (the nodes are centred and scaled at each unit's
posterior mode and curvature, so the rule stays accurate for long panels where
a fixed rule aliases). The unit is the observation of the likelihood: its
contributions, the robust standard errors, the bootstrap, and `vuong()` are
over units, while `fit_stats()` and the information criteria count cases.


``` r
set.seed(6)
G <- 200; T <- 5; unit <- rep(seq_len(G), each = T)
x1 <- rnorm(G * T); u <- cbind(rnorm(G, 0, 0.8), rnorm(G, 0, 1.2))
V <- cbind(0, 0.3 + 0.8 * x1 + u[unit, 1], -0.2 - 0.6 * x1 + u[unit, 2])
P <- exp(V) / rowSums(exp(V))
y <- apply(P, 1, function(p) sample.int(3, 1, prob = p))
dr <- data.frame(y = factor(c("a", "b", "c")[y]), x1, unit = factor(unit))
mre <- remnl(y ~ x1, data = dr, unit = "unit")
summary(mre)
#> Multinomial logit with random alternative-specific intercepts (200 units, 12-point Gauss-Hermite per dimension) 
#> Call: remnl(formula = y ~ x1, data = dr, unit = "unit")
#> Alternatives: a, b, c  (base: a)
#> 
#> Outcome equations (alternative:term):
#>               Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> b:(Intercept)  0.33107    0.09992   3.313 0.000922 ***
#> b:x1           0.91739    0.10744   8.539  < 2e-16 ***
#> c:(Intercept) -0.25632    0.13359  -1.919 0.055027 .  
#> c:x1          -0.59009    0.11597  -5.088 3.62e-07 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Random alternative-specific intercepts: standard deviations (no z test: sd = 0 is on the boundary; use lr_test() against the mnl() fit):
#>      Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)
#> sd:b   0.6918     0.1573      NA       NA
#> sd:c   1.0529     0.1601      NA       NA
#> 
#> Standard errors: analytic. Log-likelihood -946.996 on 6 parameters, 1000 cases. AIC 1905.99, BIC 1935.44.
lr_test(mnl(y ~ x1, data = dr), mre)
#> Likelihood-ratio test
#>   LR = 48.7747 on 2 df, p = 2.563e-11
```

The restriction \(\sigma = 0\) is on the boundary of the parameter space, so
the chi-square p-value of the likelihood-ratio test is conservative.

The random intercepts are independent relative to the base alternative, so
with three or more alternatives the base is part of the model. Relative to
another base they would be correlated, which the diagonal model does not
represent. A fit with another `ref` is a different model, with its own
log-likelihood and its own test against the logit (`?remnl` has an example).
The data above were simulated with alternative `a` free of a random intercept,
and `a` is the base.

At two
alternatives the model is the binomial generalized linear mixed model with a
random intercept, and the package's verification ledger records agreement with
`lme4::glmer(nAGQ = 25)` across panel lengths from six to fifty cases per unit
and standard deviations of one and two: within 1.2e-3 in the log-likelihood
with the default 12 quadrature points (and 6e-5 at fifty cases per unit), and
within 2e-6 with 40 points; the package's tests check both settings.

## Fixed effects and the split-panel jackknife

`fe = "unit"` adds alternative-specific constants per unit. A unit that never
chooses an alternative has that constant at minus infinity; the fit treats the
alternative as unavailable to the unit, which is the limiting likelihood, and
says so; a unit that never chooses the base alternative has the base
unavailable to it and one constant fewer, and a unit with a constant choice
drops out. Maximum-likelihood unit constants carry the incidental-parameters
bias in nonlinear models, of order \(1/T\): with six to twelve cases per unit
the slopes are inflated by 15-30 percent. `bias_correct = "jackknife"` removes the
leading term by the split-panel jackknife of Dhaene and Jochmans (2015): the
model is refit on the first and second halves of every unit's cases (rows are
split in the order supplied, which should be temporal order) and the corrected
slope is twice the full-sample estimate minus the mean of the half-panel
estimates.


``` r
set.seed(7)
G <- 200; T <- 12; unit <- rep(seq_len(G), each = T)
x1 <- rnorm(G * T); x2 <- rnorm(G * T)
a <- cbind(rnorm(G), rnorm(G))
V <- cbind(0, 0.3 + 0.8 * x1 - 0.5 * x2 + a[unit, 1], -0.2 - 0.6 * x1 + 0.7 * x2 + a[unit, 2])
P <- exp(V) / rowSums(exp(V))
y <- apply(P, 1, function(p) sample.int(3, 1, prob = p))
dfe <- data.frame(y = factor(c("a", "b", "c")[y]), x1, x2, unit = factor(unit))
mfe <- mnl(y ~ x1 + x2, data = dfe, fe = "unit", bias_correct = "jackknife")
rbind(ML = mfe$uncorrected$coefficients[c("b:x1", "b:x2", "c:x1", "c:x2")],
      jackknife = coef(mfe)[c("b:x1", "b:x2", "c:x1", "c:x2")],
      truth = c(0.8, -0.5, -0.6, 0.7))
#>                b:x1       b:x2       c:x1      c:x2
#> ML        0.9279685 -0.6552988 -0.7673811 0.6876658
#> jackknife 0.7939230 -0.5883886 -0.6712075 0.6089599
#> truth     0.8000000 -0.5000000 -0.6000000 0.7000000
```

Three of the four corrected slopes move towards the values the data were
drawn from and one moves away, which is what one sample of a noisy correction
looks like; the simulations described below are the evidence about the method. (The unit
constants are nuisance parameters: the printed summary reports only their
number, `texreg` tables leave them out by default (`include.fe = TRUE` shows
them), and `tidy()` lists them.)

The correction is valid only when the two halves estimate the same parameter
(time homogeneity), so it is refused, with a warning naming the check, when
the half-panel slopes disagree beyond the noise of placebo splits (random
halves of every unit's cases that ignore the time order) or when the full
fit's residuals trend with time within units (the cure for the latter is a
time control in the formula: a trend, since period dummies are not
identified within the half panels). A refused fit keeps `bias_correct =
"none"` and the reason in `$jackknife_refused`, which `summary()` prints. The
placebo splits have the time split's structure, so under time homogeneity
the two disagreements are on the same footing at every panel length, and the
threshold, 2.5 times the placebo noise, was calibrated by simulation (150
units, \(J = 3\), \(T = 6, 10, 20\)) as the smallest value on a grid that
kept the refusal rate of time-homogeneous panels at or below 5 percent at
every \(T\), under a rule written down before the simulations were run and
checked on fresh seeds. Regime changes were refused in 92 percent of the
simulated panels at \(T = 6\) and in all of them at \(T = 10\) and 20, and
omitted trends in all panels at \(T = 10\) and 20 but in only about half at
\(T = 6\), since six cases per unit carry little evidence of a trend. The
verification ledger in the repository reports the refusal rates and the
signed bias, root mean squared error, and interval coverage of both
estimators. The correction removes the leading \(1/T\) term only, so in very
short panels it over-corrects: at \(T = 6\) and 10 the corrected slopes keep
part of the maximum-likelihood bias with the opposite sign; at \(T = 20\) the
maximum-likelihood slopes are still biased by several percent and the
corrected ones by much less. At every panel length it lowers the root mean
squared error and brings Wald intervals closer to their nominal coverage.

`mundlak()` is the correlated-random-effects alternative for short panels: it
adds the unit means of the covariates to the formula. Fit with `remnl()` the
augmented model recovers the within-unit slopes; a pooled `mnl()` fit of the
same formula with `cluster = "unit"` gives population-averaged slopes, which
are attenuated by the unit-effect variance (here by about a quarter), the
usual behaviour of a pooled nonlinear model.


``` r
mk <- mundlak(y ~ x1 + x2, data = dfe, unit = "unit")
print(mk$formula, showEnv = FALSE)
#> y ~ x1 + x2 + x1_mean + x2_mean
mre2 <- remnl(mk$formula, data = mk$data, unit = "unit")
mm <- mnl(mk$formula, data = mk$data, cluster = "unit")
rbind(remnl = coef(mre2)[c("b:x1", "b:x2", "c:x1", "c:x2")],
      pooled = coef(mm)[c("b:x1", "b:x2", "c:x1", "c:x2")],
      truth = c(0.8, -0.5, -0.6, 0.7))
#>             b:x1       b:x2       c:x1      c:x2
#> remnl  0.8221589 -0.5878710 -0.6914936 0.6146194
#> pooled 0.6088783 -0.4414858 -0.5039616 0.4460536
#> truth  0.8000000 -0.5000000 -0.6000000 0.7000000
```

## Choosing among the families

* The logit is nested in the nested logit, the HEV, and the random-intercept
  model: use `lr_test()` (with the boundary caveat for the random intercepts).
* The probit is not nested with any of them: use `vuong()` or
  `compare_models()`.
* `compare_models()` lines up log-likelihoods, degrees of freedom, and
  information criteria for any set of fits to the same cases.


``` r
compare_models(logit = mnl(y ~ x1, data = dr), random_intercepts = mre)
#>              model
#>              logit
#>  random_intercepts
#>                                                                                                             type
#>                                                                                                Multinomial logit
#>  Multinomial logit with random alternative-specific intercepts (200 units, 12-point Gauss-Hermite per dimension)
#>  inflate    n df   loglik      AIC      BIC mcfadden converged boundary
#>          1000  4 -971.383 1950.766 1970.397    0.099      TRUE    FALSE
#>          1000  6 -946.996 1905.991 1935.438    0.122      TRUE    FALSE
#>  ill_conditioned n_modes
#>            FALSE       1
#>            FALSE       1
```

Bhat, C.R. (1995). A heteroscedastic extreme value model of intercity travel
mode choice. *Transportation Research Part B*, 29, 471-483.

Dhaene, G. and Jochmans, K. (2015). Split-panel jackknife estimation of
fixed-effect models. *Review of Economic Studies*, 82, 991-1030.

Keane, M.P. (1992). A note on identification in the multinomial probit model.
*Journal of Business and Economic Statistics*, 10, 193-200.

McFadden, D. (1978). Modelling the choice of residential location. In A.
Karlqvist et al. (eds), *Spatial Interaction Theory and Planning Models*,
75-96. North-Holland.

Train, K.E. (2009). *Discrete Choice Methods with Simulation*, 2nd ed.
Cambridge University Press.
